text.title: How Lichens Colonise Bare Rock
text.body:
A lichen is not a single organism but a partnership between a fungus and a partner that can photosynthesise, usually a green alga or a cyanobacterium. The fungus forms the body of the lichen and anchors it to a surface, while the partner produces sugars from sunlight. This arrangement allows lichens to survive in places where neither partner could live alone, including bare rock surfaces exposed to wind, frost and intense sun.

Lichens tolerate such conditions partly because they can dry out almost completely and become dormant, then resume growth within minutes of being moistened by rain or dew. As they grow, they slowly break down the rock beneath them. Their tiny root-like threads penetrate small cracks, and the acids they release dissolve certain minerals.

Over decades, this weathering produces a thin layer of mineral particles. When lichens die, their remains mix with these particles to form a primitive soil. Mosses and small plants can then take root, which is why ecologists describe lichens as pioneer species.

options: It produces sugars from sunlight.
It attaches the lichen to a surface.
It shields the alga from frost.
It releases minerals into the air.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the fungus 'forms the body of the lichen and anchors it to a surface'.

questions.explanation: Dried-out lichens stop growing and later 'resume growth', so 'dormant' means inactive.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 lists 'wind, frost and intense sun'; a lack of oxygen is never mentioned.

options: To contrast them with lichens' ability to survive drought
To give examples of other partnerships involving fungi
To explain why lichens die after several decades
To show what can grow once lichens have produced soil
questions.explanation: Mosses and plants 'can then take root' in the primitive soil, which shows why lichens are called pioneer species.

options: It breaks down rock faster than the fungus does.
It forms the main body of the lichen.
It could not survive on bare rock without the fungus.
It needs soil before it can begin to grow.
questions.explanation: Lichens survive on bare rock 'where neither partner could live alone', so the photosynthetic partner depends on the fungus there.

text.title: Why Some Trees Lose Their Leaves in Autumn
text.body:
In many parts of the world, trees such as maples and oaks drop all of their leaves in autumn. These trees are called deciduous trees. Losing leaves may seem wasteful, but it helps the trees survive the winter.

Leaves are useful in summer because they use sunlight to make food. However, they also lose a lot of water through tiny holes on their surface. In winter, the ground is often frozen, so roots cannot take in much water. A tree that kept its broad leaves would lose more water than it could replace. Heavy snow on leaves could also break branches.

Before the leaves fall, the tree takes back useful nutrients from them and stores them in its branches and roots. The green colour fades, and yellow and orange colours that were hidden all summer become visible. Finally, a layer of special cells forms where each leaf joins the branch, and the leaf drops off. In spring, the tree grows new leaves.

text.body:
Dear all,

Kestrel Hall has been sold, and the new owners will not be renting it out after December. After visiting four alternatives, the committee has chosen the music room at Fairfield Secondary School. It is smaller, so we will rehearse in two sections on alternate weeks, with the full choir meeting only on the last Tuesday of each month. The school also charges more than the hall did. Rather than raise the membership fee for everyone, we propose a voluntary 'supporter' rate for those able to pay extra. This will be put to a vote at the annual meeting on 2 December; members who cannot attend may vote by email beforehand. I appreciate this is a lot of change at once, but I'd rather be upfront now than surprise you in January.

Best wishes,
Ruth Okafor, Musical Director

text.title: The Puzzle of Desert Pavement
text.body:
Across large areas of the world's deserts, the ground is covered by a tightly packed layer of pebbles, often only one or two stones thick. Beneath this surface, surprisingly, there is usually fine, almost stone-free silt. For much of the twentieth century, geologists explained this arrangement through deflation: wind, they argued, gradually carried away sand and dust, leaving behind stones too heavy to move, which settled into an interlocking armour.

Later fieldwork challenged this account. If wind had simply removed fine material from mixed sediment, the soil beneath the surface should still contain plenty of stones, yet it rarely does. Moreover, some pavements lie on lava flows only a few thousand years old, and dating showed that their stones had remained at the surface ever since the flows cooled. An alternative explanation therefore gained support: windblown dust settles between the stones, is washed beneath them by rain, and slowly accumulates, so that the pebbles are not left behind but raised up on a growing layer of silt.

Most researchers now accept that both processes operate, although their relative importance varies from site to site.

questions.prompt: The word "account" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: explanation
calculation
customer
measurement
questions.explanation: 'This account' refers back to the deflation explanation described at the end of paragraph 1.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention lava flows in paragraph 2?
options: To show where desert pavements are most common
To present evidence that the stones were never buried
To explain why some pavements are one stone thick
To describe how silt forms from volcanic rock
questions.explanation: Dating showed the stones on young lava flows 'had remained at the surface ever since the flows cooled', evidence against the idea that they were uncovered by wind.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT part of the alternative explanation described in paragraph 2?
options: Dust is carried in by the wind.
Rain moves dust beneath the stones.
Wind removes the lighter particles.
Silt builds up under the pebbles.
questions.explanation: Wind removing fine particles is the older deflation theory; the alternative says dust is added, washed under the stones and accumulates.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the deflation theory would the author most likely agree with?
options: It cannot, on its own, explain the silt beneath pavements.
It has been completely abandoned by researchers.
It was first proposed after studies of lava flows.
It explains why pavements form only in hot deserts.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows deflation does not fit the stone-free silt, yet paragraph 3 says 'both processes operate', so it is incomplete rather than abandoned.

options: It is made mainly of lava.

It is several metres deep.
It contains very few stones.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'Beneath this surface, surprisingly, there is usually fine, almost stone-free silt'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a zoology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today we're looking at a question that puzzled people for centuries: how do migratory birds find their way, sometimes across thousands of kilometres? The short answer is that they don't rely on just one system. They use several, almost like backups. First, there's the sun. Many birds can tell direction from the sun's position, and they adjust for the time of day using their internal clock. But a lot of songbirds migrate at night. So what do they use? Well, experiments in planetariums showed that young birds learn the pattern of stars rotating around the North Star. When researchers changed the projected sky, the birds changed direction. Then there's the Earth's magnetic field. Birds seem able to sense it, which helps on cloudy nights when neither sun nor stars are visible. And close to the end of the journey, landmarks such as coastlines and rivers, and even smells, take over. Now, here's what I find remarkable. Young birds on their first migration often fly alone, without a parent to follow. So the basic direction, at least, seems to be inherited rather than taught.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an architecture class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: OK, let's talk about one of the defining features of Gothic cathedrals: the flying buttress. Builders in the twelfth century wanted two things that seemed to contradict each other. They wanted very tall buildings, and they wanted huge windows full of stained glass. The problem is that a tall stone vault pushes outward on the walls. Earlier churches, in the Romanesque style, dealt with this by making the walls really thick, which left room for only small windows.

audio.speaker: Student
audio.text: So the buttress pushes back against the wall?

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Exactly. A flying buttress is an arch that leans against the upper wall from the outside and carries that outward force down to a heavy pier on the ground. Because the wall no longer has to do all the work, it can be thinner, and large parts of it can be glass. Think of someone leaning a hand against a tall bookcase to keep it from tipping. Now, not everyone has admired buttresses. Some later critics thought they looked like scaffolding that had never been taken down. But many builders decorated them with carvings and small spires, turning a structural necessity into part of the style.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a history of technology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Today let's look at the early history of the bicycle. The first one appeared in Germany in 1817. It was made of wood and, surprisingly, it had no pedals. Riders sat on it and pushed along the ground with their feet, a bit like a child's balance bike. In the 1860s, pedals were added, but they were attached directly to the front wheel. To go faster, makers made the front wheel bigger and bigger. This led to the penny-farthing, with a huge front wheel and a tiny back one. It was fast, but it was also dangerous. Riders sat very high, and if they hit a stone, they could fall over the handlebars. Then, in the 1880s, came the safety bicycle. It had two wheels of the same size and a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel. This design was much easier to ride, and it's basically the bicycle we still use today. Soon, many more people, including many women, began cycling for work and for fun.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why cycling became a popular sport
How bicycles are made today
How the bicycle's design changed over time
Why the first bicycle was made in Germany
questions.explanation: The professor describes three designs in order: the wooden bicycle, the penny-farthing and the safety bicycle.

questions.prompt: What was unusual about the first bicycle?
options: It had no pedals.
It had three wheels.
It was made of metal.
It used a chain.
questions.explanation: It was made of wood and 'had no pedals'.

options: Its wheels often broke.
Riders sat very high up.
It had no handlebars.
It was too slow on hills.
questions.explanation: Riders sat very high and could fall over the handlebars if they hit a stone.

questions.prompt: What did the safety bicycle have?

A chain to the back wheel
questions.explanation: It had 'a chain that connected the pedals to the back wheel'.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in an anthropology class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Let's turn to gift exchange. In everyday speech, a gift is something given freely, with no strings attached. Anthropologists, though, have long argued that this is almost never the case. The French scholar Marcel Mauss, writing in the 1920s, pointed out that in many societies a gift creates three obligations: to give, to receive, and to give back. Refusing a gift can be read as refusing a relationship. Now, the return gift usually isn't immediate, and it's rarely identical. If I hand you back the same thing straight away, it looks less like generosity and more like I'm settling a bill, closing the account, so to speak. The delay is what keeps the relationship going. You can see a version of this in the famous kula exchange in the Trobriand Islands, where shell necklaces and armbands circulate between islands for years. Nobody keeps them for long, so what's really being exchanged? Well, partnerships and reputation. Closer to home, think about dinner invitations. If friends have you over twice and you never invite them back, nobody sends you an invoice. But you'll probably notice the invitations drying up.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of the talk?
options: Traditional gifts are worth more than modern ones.
Gifts create obligations that sustain relationships.
Most anthropologists now reject Mauss's theory.
Shell necklaces were an early form of money.
questions.explanation: The professor argues that gifts are rarely free because they create obligations to give back, which keep relationships going.

questions.prompt: What does the professor imply about returning an identical gift immediately?
options: It is the most polite way to show thanks.
It is common practice in the Trobriand Islands.
It makes the original gift more valuable.
It may signal a wish to end the relationship.
questions.explanation: It looks like 'closing the account', and since the delay keeps the relationship going, an instant return suggests ending it.

questions.prompt: Why does the professor mention the kula exchange?
options: To show that the objects matter less than the ties
To give an example of trade based on money
To show how valuable shell jewellery once was
To contrast island customs with Mauss's theory
questions.explanation: Nobody keeps the shells for long, so what is really exchanged is 'partnerships and reputation'.

questions.prompt: What does the professor mean when she says "nobody sends you an invoice"?
options: Friends prefer to split the cost of meals.

Most people forget who invited them last.
questions.explanation: No one asks for repayment openly, yet the invitations stop, so the obligation exists without being stated.

tasks.context: Listen to part of a talk in a physics class.

audio.speaker: Professor
audio.text: Why do some concert halls sound wonderful and others, frankly, disappointing? A lot of it comes down to reverberation: the sound that keeps bouncing around a room after the musicians stop. Acousticians measure reverberation time, roughly how long it takes a sound to fade away. For a lecture hall, you want it short, under a second, or the words blur together. For orchestral music, around two seconds is often considered ideal. It makes the music feel full and warm. But reverberation isn't the whole story. Shape matters too. Many of the halls musicians love most, like the Musikverein in Vienna, are tall, narrow rectangles, the so-called shoebox design. Sound bounces off the side walls and reaches listeners from the sides, which gives a feeling of being surrounded by the music. Wide, fan-shaped halls were popular in the twentieth century because they fit more seats with good sightlines. Unfortunately, the side walls are too far away to send much sound back. So you can see the orchestra beautifully and, well, you hear rather less of it than you'd like. Designers today often try to get the best of both, with seating split into terraces, each with its own nearby walls.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: How orchestras adapt to different halls
Why lecture halls need long reverberation
The history of concert halls in Vienna
Features that affect how a hall sounds
questions.explanation: The professor explains how reverberation time and hall shape make halls sound better or worse.

questions.prompt: Why is a short reverberation time preferred in a lecture hall?
options: So that speech stays clear
So that more seats can fit
So that music sounds warmer
So that listeners feel surrounded
questions.explanation: Without a short time, 'the words blur together'.

questions.prompt: What is the professor's attitude toward fan-shaped halls?
options: He thinks they are ideal for orchestras.
He feels their problems are exaggerated.
He is critical of their sound despite their benefits.
He admires them mainly for their capacity.
questions.explanation: He grants that they give many seats and good views, but says 'unfortunately' you hear less of the orchestra.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the terraced designs mentioned at the end?
options: They reduce the number of seats in a hall.
They try to combine capacity with side reflections.
They copy the shape of fan-shaped halls exactly.
They were first used in the Musikverein.
questions.explanation: 'The best of both' means keeping many seats while giving each section nearby walls that reflect sound.

items.explanation: Subject + verb + noun phrase; the adjective goes before 'ones': No, mine are the black ones.

items.prompt: Why were you late for the seminar?
items.explanation: Choose a/an by sound, not spelling: 'an hour' (silent h, vowel sound) and 'a university' (starts with a /ju/ consonant sound): It took me an hour to find a university parking space.

items.prompt: Did you catch the train to the airport?
items.explanation: Past perfect for the earlier event (the train leaving), past simple after 'by the time' for the later one: No, it had already left by the time I got to the station.

items.prompt: Can your younger brother drive us to the festival?
items.explanation: The adverb 'enough' comes after an adjective (old enough, not enough old), followed by a to-infinitive: No, he isn't old enough to have a licence.

items.prompt: What happened to the team meeting on Friday?
items.explanation: With a phrasal verb, an object pronoun must go between the verb and the particle: 'called it off', never 'called off it': The manager called it off because half the team was ill.

items.prompt: Who is the woman in that photo?
items.explanation: 'whose + noun' starts the relative clause, then subject + verb + object, and the preposition stays at the end: She's the scientist whose research I told you about.

items.prompt: I need to phone the registration office about my form.
items.explanation: An indirect question uses statement order (subject before verb): 'why my application was rejected', not 'why was my application rejected'.

items.prompt: Why have you borrowed so many books about insects?
items.explanation: 'an essay' (one essay, vowel sound); 'the role of ...' is made specific by the of-phrase; 'bees' in general takes no article: I'm writing an essay on the role of bees.

items.prompt: Why did you nearly miss your flight?
items.explanation: Indirect question in statement order plus past perfect for the earlier action: I couldn't remember where I had put my passport (not 'where had I put').

items.prompt: Did you get caught in that storm last night?
items.explanation: After 'No sooner' at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject (inversion), and the pattern continues with 'than': No sooner had I got home than it started to pour.
